title: Lamentations 4:17–22
context: Lamentations 4:17–22 shifts to the community speaking as “we.” They looked in vain for help from a nation that could not save, were hunted in their own streets, and were chased by pursuers swifter than eagles on the mountains and in the wilderness. The LORD’s anointed, the breath of their nostrils, under whose shadow they hoped to live, was captured. Many identify him with Zedekiah, whose flight and capture are told in 2 Kings 25:4–7, Jeremiah 39:4–7, and 52:7–11; these accounts are named without harmonizing, and the poem does not name him. In the last two verses the poet turns to Edom and tells it to rejoice for now, because the cup of judgment will pass to it too. The poet tells Zion that her punishment is complete and she will not be exiled again, while Edom’s sins will be uncovered. Edom’s hostility at Jerusalem’s fall is also named in Psalm 137:7 and Obadiah 10–14.

verses.text: Our eyes still fail, looking in vain for our help. In our watching we have watched for a nation that could not save.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says their eyes failed looking in vain for help, watching for a nation that could not save. Arminian readers see misplaced trust in foreign allies, which the prophets warned against repeatedly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the futility of trusting human powers instead of God. Both traditions note that many connect the nation with Egypt (compare Jeremiah 37:5–10), though the poem does not name it.

verses.text: They hunt our steps, so that we can’t go in our streets. Our end is near. Our days are fulfilled, for our end has come.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says the enemy hunted their steps so they could not go in their streets, and their end has come. Arminians see the hopelessness of life under siege, when even the city’s streets were unsafe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as expressing the certainty of the city’s fall. Both traditions read the repeated words about the end as the community’s confession that God’s warnings had come true.

verses.text: Our pursuers were swifter than the eagles of the sky. They chased us on the mountains. They set an ambush for us in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says their pursuers were swifter than eagles, chasing them on the mountains and setting ambushes in the wilderness. Arminian readers see the impossibility of escape, as the enemy hunted down those who fled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of eagles as stressing the enemy’s speed. Both traditions note that the verse may recall the flight from the city described in 2 Kings 25:4–5, while the poem does not give details.

verses.text: The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the LORD, was taken in their pits; of whom we said, under his shadow we will live among the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: The community says the LORD’s anointed, the breath of their nostrils, under whose shadow they hoped to live, was captured in their pits. Arminians see the people’s grief at losing their king, in whom they had placed their hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the loss of the Davidic king as a great sorrow. Both traditions note that many identify the king with Zedekiah (2 Kings 25:4–7; Jeremiah 39:4–7; 52:7–11), named without harmonizing, and they observe that the people’s trust in him was misplaced, though the title remained sacred.

verses.text: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom, who dwells in the land of Uz. The cup will pass through to you also. You will be drunken, and will make yourself naked.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet tells the daughter of Edom, living in the land of Uz, to rejoice, but warns that the cup will pass to her too. Arminian readers see God’s justice reaching the nations who rejoiced at Jerusalem’s fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign rule over all nations. Both traditions compare Psalm 137:7 and Obadiah 10–14 on Edom’s hostility and the cup of judgment in Jeremiah 25:15–21, and note that the location of Uz is uncertain.

verses.text: The punishment of your iniquity is accomplished, daughter of Zion. He will no more carry you away into captivity. He will visit your iniquity, daughter of Edom. He will uncover your sins.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet tells Zion her punishment is complete and she will not be exiled again, while Edom’s iniquity will be visited and uncovered. Arminians see a turning point of hope, as Zion’s suffering reaches its limit while judgment moves to her enemy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s faithfulness in ending his people’s punishment. Both traditions hold this as shared ground about hope after judgment, and they compare the comfort of Isaiah 40:2.
